name: Methyl hyaluronate

lead:
Methyl hyaluronate is a hyaluronic acid (HA) derivative in which the carboxyl groups of HA carry a methyl group. HA is a major component of skin that binds water and helps tissue repair, and it is common in skincare and in injectable fillers.
Chemical modification of HA, including esterification, is studied to improve how well it penetrates or lasts. Wikipedia describes these modifications in general terms; published studies of methyl hyaluronate as a skincare ingredient are not covered here.

paras: In general, HA products are used as topical serums and moisturisers or as injectables given by clinicians.
No specific safety data for methyl hyaluronate are given here. For HA fillers in general, Wikipedia lists pain, bruising, redness, vascular occlusion and, rarely, granulomatous reactions.

angle.text: As an HA derivative, it falls within the group of ingredients used for skin hydration. Specific benefits of the methyl ester form are not documented.

lead: Methyl hyaluronate refers to a methyl ester of hyaluronic acid, one of several chemically modified forms of HA.[1]

HA is a major component of skin that helps with tissue repair, and it is a common skincare ingredient; UV exposure reduces dermal HA production and speeds its breakdown.[1] People use HA products for hydration and to soften the look of lines.
Modifications at HA's carboxyl, hydroxyl and N-acetyl groups, including esterification, are made to improve biocompatibility, permeation and sustained release.[1]

paras: Hyaluronic acid can be modified at its carboxyl, hydroxyl and N-acetyl groups; esterification is one such modification, and cross-linking with agents such as BDDE makes longer-lasting gels.[1] Sodium hyaluronate is the sodium salt form.[1]
Karl Meyer and John Palmer first isolated HA from cow vitreous humor in 1934, and Pharmacia developed the first biomedical HA product, Healon, for eye surgery in the 1970s and 1980s.[1]

timeline.event: Meyer and Palmer first isolate HA.[1]
